# Asset sources

For licences, receipts and credits of third-party assets, and where free game art, icons, palettes, plugins and animations come from.

## Core

- Licences: CC0 needs nothing (credit is a courtesy). CC-BY and OGA-BY need the credit the author asks for. BY-SA and GPL make the derived asset carry the same licence; GPL art in a closed game needs the user's decision. NC never goes into paid, monetised or commercial work. Quote a custom or unclear licence verbatim to the user rather than summarising it.
- Each grabbed asset gets a receipt `<asset-id>.json` beside its files (`source`, `id`, `title`, `url`, `authors`, `license`, `licenseUrl`, `attribution`, `acquiredAt`, `files`) and a line in the project's `CREDITS`: title, author, source URL, licence.
- `voyager assets search <words> [--type texture|hdri|model|icon|music|pack] [--source …]` searches Poly Haven (CC0 textures, HDRIs, models), ambientCG (CC0 materials, HDRIs), Kenney (CC0 packs), game-icons.net and Incompetech; `voyager assets download <source>:<id> [--resolution 2k]` saves under `assets/<source>/<id>/` with the receipt and the `CREDITS` line. Poly Haven asks that users are told its assets come from Poly Haven.
- Kenney (kenney.nl): CC0 whole packs (2D, 3D, UI, audio, textures); search matches pack names and categories only. Packs include `License.txt`.
- Animated CC0 sets: Quaternius [Ultimate Animated Character Pack](https://quaternius.com/packs/ultimatedanimatedcharacter.html) and [Ultimate Animated Animal Pack](https://quaternius.com/packs/ultimateanimatedanimals.html), Kenney [Animated Characters Protagonists](https://kenney.nl/assets/animated-characters-protagonists), and three.js [RobotExpressive](https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/tree/dev/examples/models/gltf/RobotExpressive). fal’s [Meshy](https://fal.ai/models/meshy/v7.1/image-to-3d/api) `meshy/v7.1/image-to-3d` auto-rigs generated humanoids with `enable_rigging: true`; animation presets use `enable_animation: true` and `animation_action_id`.
- game-icons.net: CC BY 3.0 (a few authors CC0), credited per icon's author. Each SVG is a black square path under a white icon path; recolour or drop them via `fill`.
- Incompetech: Kevin MacLeod's music, CC BY 4.0 with his credit text; fetch single tracks only.
- Lospec: `https://lospec.com/palette-list/<slug>.json` returns name, author (sometimes empty; the palette page names the creator) and hex colours. Credit "<palette> by <author> (Lospec)".
- Godot Asset Library: keyless JSON at `godotengine.org/asset-library/api/asset?filter=…&godot_version=4.3` (without `godot_version` it returns nothing); `cost` holds the licence, `/asset/<id>` gives `download_url`. Plugins and scripts, not art. The new Godot Asset Store (beta, no public API) is replacing it.
- OpenGameArt: no API. Search pages (`/art-search-advanced?keys=…`) only; robots.txt sets a 10 s crawl delay and disallows `/search/`. Licences (often several, including SA and GPL) and the attribution text are on each content page.
- Mixamo: Adobe's terms forbid access other than through its interface and any data mining, so the user downloads in their own browser; Voyager imports and rigs the FBX. Raw characters and animations are not redistributable.
- itch.io: no search API (every endpoint needs auth and covers your own account); tag pages have RSS (`itch.io/game-assets/free/tag-<tag>.xml`) without licences. Licences are free text per page; the user downloads, and pays where needed.

# Rights and delivery

For asset rights, credits, subtitles and delivery checks.

## Core

- Deliver a `CREDITS` file naming every third-party asset (samples, music, fonts, images, the voice engine) with its source and licence; credit on screen where a licence requires it; tell the user `CREDITS` lists the licences and the material is their responsibility.
- When anything is spoken, offer an `.srt` in one line.
- `voyager media review FILE` measures loudness but flags only a true peak above 0 dBTP (clipping): check `audio.integratedLUFS` near −14 and `audio.truePeakDBTP` at or below −1 yourself. It also checks black frames and duration. Re-level with two-pass `loudnorm` (`TP=-1`, `linear=true`, the first pass's measured values) and review again before presenting.
- To judge continuous motion, sync or how a clip sounds, use a video-understanding model with `voyager models run`; load `choose-media-model/references/understanding.md` for the paid upload route.

# Typography

For authoring text or changing fonts, layout or output size.

## Core

- Author exact words, numbers and supplied logos as controlled text or overlays;
  inspect the exported file rather than relying on generated imagery to spell.
- Write English copy in US spelling unless the user, their brand kit or the
  project uses another variety.
- Verify the actual renderer has the faces you use; a brand kit's supported-font
  flag is not proof of availability.
- Protect descenders,
  accents and cap height from clipping, including inside masks and line boxes.
- Use the editor integration skill for font loading. For a brand's fonts in Remotion or
  HyperFrames that is the generated brand-fonts helper, not hand-written `@font-face`;
  if it reports a substitute, say so to the user.
- Renderers add no motion blur: fine print and 1–2 px hairlines shimmer in fast moves; keep them out of fast moves or enlarge them.

# CAD model to cinematic product animation in Blender

## Goal

A short widescreen film of {PRODUCT} built from the real {CAD_FILE}: travelling cameras, macro close-ups, motion at its real joints, a continuous exploded view and reassembly, restrained titles and music. Geometry stays exactly as modelled; the CAD's accuracy is the point, so only the real joints move and exploded spacing is labelled as illustrative.

## How it came together

Fidelity to the source drives the early choices. Native assembly formats keep placements and colours better than exported meshes; convert with a CAD kernel if Blender can't open them, and check part count and bounds against the source before going further. Units must be physically correct because depth of field and texture scale depend on them. Read the actual licence and record credits.

Rig from the assembly's own joint anchors and axes (cross-check any kinematics files); exploded groups follow logical subassemblies. Presentation materials in {FINISH} got subtle, non-repeating grain, and shaped key/rim light held the finish colour. The user approved a whole-product still, a lighting still and the shot plan before anything long was rendered, then a cheap full-cut preview with temp music.

Titles rendered separately stay sharp under lens blur; reuse the user's music if they have it. Ask before long or paid renders, and render per shot so a crash costs one section.

## Example request

> Make a {LENGTH}-second {ASPECT} product animation of {PRODUCT} from {CAD_FILE}, accurate to the CAD. Finish: {FINISH}. Setting: {ENVIRONMENT}. Show real joint motion, an exploded view and close-ups of {FEATURES}. Camera style like {REFERENCE}. Music: {MUSIC}.

## What worked in the original (starting points, not rules)

- A 517-part open-source robot arm converted from native FreeCAD; satin red/black finish in a white factory set; 34 s at 21:9.
- f/1.4-1.8 macros with ray-cast focus on visible surfaces; stopped down for the exploded hold.
- Cycles at 32 samples, 1680x720, about 35-40 min on a laptop GPU.

## Watch out for

- Unit mismatches break depth of field and texture grain.
- Focusing on part origins leaves macros blurred; focus on the visible face.
- The separation and exploded hold must be one continuous camera, or parts appear to jump.
- Broad fill flattens the product and washes out colour.
- Motion blur can pulse unevenly; turn it off per shot if needed.
- Local GPU renders may crash or flash single frames; render per shot, resume, rerender only bad frames.
- After the final, recheck that part count still matches the source.
- "More photoreal" isn't always preferred; keep every approved look.
